text: Good afternoon. I'm calling this meeting of the Finance and Operations Committee to order. I am here with my colleagues, Ms. Ricardi and Mr. Pepper. I was just informed we do not have public comment. We will next go to the minutes. May I have a motion to approve the minutes of the October 20th, 2026 Finance and Operations Committee meeting? So moved. Second. Thank you.

It has been moved and seconded to approve the minutes for the October 2026 Finance and Operations Committee meeting. All those in favor say aye. Aye. Aye. Aye. We will now move to action items. Or wait, did I miss something? Oops, I'm sorry. Consent agenda. We will now move on to our consent agenda. May I have a motion to approve the consent agenda? So moved. Second.

Thank you very much. It has been moved and seconded to approve the consent agenda. All those in favor say aye. Aye. Aye. Aye. We will now move on to our action items, starting with item 5.01, Support Surfaces Grant of Stream Restoration and Floodplain Easements at Riverbend Middle School and Potomac Falls High School. May I have a motion to approve 5.01?

Madam Chair, I move that the Finance and Operations Committee place this item on the school board meeting consent agenda and recommend that the Loudoun County School Board approve the grant of the stream restoration and floodplain easements to the Board of Supervisors of Loudoun County, Virginia, at Riverbend Middle School and Potomac Falls High School. Further, the chair of the school board is authorized to sign the deeds of easement upon presentation. Amy. Second.

Thank you both. The item is being presented by Mr. Trainer, Executive Director, Chief of Facilities. Thank you. Thank you. Board, I don't have any additional information. The last meeting you had asked for this to be put on as an action item instead of consent so that Chair Chandler could review it. Mr. Mahoon and I met with Chair Chandler last Friday, went through it in

just a few minutes, and she had no additional questions or concerns. She's very comfortable with it. Any other discussion? No? Okay. I believe we were waiting for Chair Chandler to take a look. So with that, if there's no more discussion, we will proceed to a vote. All those in favor in sending this to the full board, say aye. Aye. Aye. I think it's consent, right? Consent. Yeah. Consent to the full board. All those in favor, say aye. Aye. Aye. Aye. Thank you.

I did it again. We will now move on to our information items, starting with item 6.01, Business and Financial Services Purchasing Authority Quarterly Report. This item is being presented by Andrea Fillow, Director of Procurement and Risk Management. Thank you. Good evening and thank you. I am here this evening to present to you our first quarter report as per Policy 4310, Purchasing Authority.

This policy was revised in June 2026 to add these reporting requirements. The reporting requirements are based on three primary data sources. The Oracle financial system provides us with the purchase order information as well as the accounts payable transactions. Bank of America Works, which provides us with the procurement card transactions, and Kev Group, which provides us with the school activity fund requirements. This report is

actually based on the various funds, with the exception of our self-insurance funds, which include our payroll and benefit transactions, along with we also did not include utilities in this report. Utilities are standard. They're exempt from the Virginia Public Procurement Act. Those dollars are properly reflected in your budget process, and for our utilities, we need to use the electric company that services where that school is located.

So there's no procurement method involved with those because it's based on the service area. The various activities that are spelled out in 4310 we've consolidated for you in the reports that were attached to the item. As per policy 4310, Section D3, the report includes the following: A summary of all notifications issued during the quarter under Section C. Individual notifications were not provided due to the

volume of those notifications, but we did provide a comprehensive first quarter activity report. This activity report is based on purchase orders that were created July, August, September of this year, and we use the purchase orders of 90% or more of the $200,000 threshold. As in the policy, the policy spells out that we are to use 90% of any threshold defined in that policy. Therefore, it was purchase orders greater

than $180,000. And what we did is that threshold captures the lowest threshold of the various reporting limits identified in the section. We also included the procurement method used for each purchase. There's a column there in per policy 4320. You'll see it listed as an LCPSIFB, RFP, cooperative, sole source. Those are all procurement methods identified in policy 4320.

In addition to purchases identified with the procurement method of exempt, which are based on the Virginia Public Procurement Act, our future reports will identify cumulative purchases from a single vendor that reach 75% of the $200,000 administrative exemption. That policy was just adopted at your school board meeting last Tuesday, therefore is not reflected in the information presented here. So that is purchase orders. That is funds that are encumbered and set aside for a purchase.

The other report I provided you is a cumulative fiscal year-to-date spending by commodity category for categories exceeding $100,000. Our current Oracle system does not allow us to easily track by NIGP commodity code. We are setting it up in Fusion for the future that it will do just that. So therefore, we pulled the data together from various resources to find where the cumulative spend for like purchases was greater than 100,000.

That once again identifies vendors where payments have exceeded $100,000 between July 1 and September 30th. I must once again remind you that is the payment amount. That is not the purchase order amount. And included in that report is also the procurement methods for the goods and services acquired, and expenditures made through the purchase card, other standard payment methods, and includes payments made using student activity funds.

The next item in the list was any corrective actions. Based on a review of the first quarter purchasing activity, no corrective actions were identified or required during the first quarter, as all purchases were made in compliance with Policy 4320, as well as the Virginia Public Procurement Act. Trend analysis, since this is our first quarter, there's no trend to analyze. Second quarter, we will work on an analysis of the first quarter to the second quarter, and then in

the future, we will provide year-over-year trends. This item, once again, is being brought before you this evening for information purposes only as required in Policy 4310. And at this time, I will open it up to any questions. Thank you. Any discussion? Go ahead, Ms. Riccardi. Thank you, Madam Chair. So, thank you guys so much for pulling this all together. And I had a chance, also I noticed that the sole source listing on the website was

updated today too, so I appreciate that being updated. I just want to go through, this is really the board's early warning system on spending. Or not even really warning system, it's just a way for us to really be able to provide some oversight. The quarterly reporting I think is going to be really interesting, but there are some shifts in the reporting that I would like to see. And so I'm going to just go through them section by section.

I think what this policy does is it really lays out three things really nicely or will eventually get to the point of laying out three things really nicely. One is just the report of the data. So what did we buy, from whom, and add it up by type. And secondly, that it'll help us analyze and catch patterns and show the work behind the conclusions that are being made. And third, really being able to compare this year with past years so we know what is normal and what's not.

And this first report gives us the first step, but not quite yet the second and the third. So this is obviously the first report that's under the revised policy, and so tonight is really about making sure that the report does what the policy asks and making sure that we're clear up front. And I want to make sure that I'm also clear up front, I should say, that I'm not questioning any of the purchases that are in here. I don't suggest in any way that there's anything going on here. I think it's a really great way for us to be able to see how we're spending money.

I think this report gives us two lists. First, on pages four through 11, so the first half of the tables that are in here, is really every purchase order of 180,000 or more written between July and September, so this first quarter of the year. And that's what we've committed to spending to. And then the second set of documents, 12 to 21, is every company that we've paid for more than $100,000 in the same quarter. And I want to make sure, number one,

that I'm right about what I've looked at. That is correct. The second report is based on a vendor spend to date report that we run. And it is based on spend by vendor, not necessarily for like purchases, because we do have vendors that we use for different types of purchases. So this is strictly based on vendor spend from July 1 to September 30th. I do ask that you

also keep in mind that with the payments, these may be payments that were issued using FY26 funds because they were carried over purchase orders. So there are cases where the purchases will carry over, like we'll get bills in July. A project won't finish till August. So these aren't necessarily FY27 expenditures per se. They are offset by a carryover budget amount to cover that purchase order along with the encumbered amount of the purchase order.

Perfect. Thanks for the clarification on that, because I forget about these things sometimes. So yeah. So there's some money that's carried over from the last year. So the first set is really organized by vendor name, and the second is really about this description and getting the descriptions of the like kind descriptors, but not necessarily of the services or products that are purchased. So got it. I think as we move forward, so the policy says that the committee is to be notified

when spending reaches certain warning levels, and I want to just put out there right now that I get that there would've been a lot of notifications had we done that. So I think that there might need to be, at some point in time in the future, some additions and changes to the policy, especially on that notification. And I guess what I want to see is as we go through this, and I looked at this, there are more than 100 companies on the payments list that are already past the 150,000 level for a single company.

So after just one quarter, we'd wind up having an enormous number of notifications. And so perhaps instead of it being notifications, we use the report as that. I'm not really sure how we're going to address that yet. But, I'm very aware that we might need to make some adjustments to the policy at some point in time in the future about the reporting pieces of that for the C3 requirement in the policy So with that question,

I would like the report to be able to show the number of purchases that reached that threshold, and then a short list of the ones that were not competitively bid with a company, what was bought, and the amount. So basically reorganizing this a little bit. So it'd be able to answer the question, how many purchases reached the warning level or that threshold last quarter, and who it was and what the dollar amount was.

So that'd be one part of it. And I'll send you an email, by the way, summarizing this, so it's all in one place. I think that'll be easier. And that's on the alert question on C3. I don't know if you guys wanted to-- If you wanted to add to that? No, I would love to, if I could jump in. We also would like a discussion about the C3 because we did struggle with that for this first quarter, and then also just

the time and ability of pulling this information. And so while it wasn't time-specific in the policy, and I think if I remember correctly, when we passed this, I think we purposefully was maybe a little vague, just knowing this was the first time and wanting to just see what it would look like. Yep. And I think we would be supportive of, if the committee was, would be to just have this be on a quarterly basis. And so could that notification be quarterly notification as

we have started here in terms of providing that information? Again, there's no additional action required from the board, and it would follow some of the other reporting that is already codified for procurement that is on a quarterly basis. So that was our first thought there. In terms of adding what you were kind of mentioning, if I understand correctly, I think that'd be something we could add relatively easily for the

next quarterly report of just adding just a summary at the bottom of each report of counts. And even maybe counts of, I think you're asking perhaps counts by the procurement method. Those would be fairly simple formulas we could throw in at the bottom that gives you a quick summary of what is being displayed. Yeah, I think that would be great. And it'd really be at the bottom of page two and the top of page three, which is that quarterly reporting, the

D1 reporting, I think is what we're talking about. Yeah, and I was thinking, just kind of big picture what I was thinking was, I think I have a couple of other things I'd like to see in this report, and so I want to get through some of those, too. And I would love for us to be able to see kind of a revised report, maybe at the next FNO meeting, just to kind of see how the information lays out and figure out how we can either tailor it a little bit more or expand it where we need

to, so that we get one report kind of formatted the way we want, and then the quarterly reports moving forward, being able to- I think the only additional information I would share is this was our interpretation of this policy. And so hearing you describe refining and tailoring and adjusting, I think it'd be a fine line in terms of what we're talking about that is required per the policy versus does this also then require an

adjustment to the policy of what we are to provide. So I just want to kind of throw that out there. Like I said, what you've described so far of adding a summary count, to me, that's just an additional layer that's relatively easy of what we have presented. And if there's anything that's more substantially different, I think we would just have to continue working with each other and then determining if that's something that falls within the purview of how the policy's currently written or if there needs to be adjustments. Yeah. I don't think I'm asking for anything that's outside of this or overly

complex. I think it's just more about laying it out so that if anybody else is looking at this, it just makes a little bit more sense than just having two big lists of vendors. And I'll just be really honest with you. I don't mind getting the two big lists because I have my AI tools that I use to help analyze a lot of this stuff to make sense of it. But I think if you're just putting lists out to the public, I think we haven't hit a couple of these requirements that are in here, and I want to just

provide a little bit more feedback on that if I could, and then we'll see what you think about it. So for C3A, and it's also part of D3B. So on the very back page, that 3B1 at the end. The policy asks staff to add up the purchases of the same kind of thing, even when they go to different companies, right?

And to flag any type of purchase that reaches the 25 or the first threshold that's on the first page here. So the threshold from 3A, the 75% of the 250,000. So the report lists all the companies out, which is great, but it never adds the like-kind things together. So if you have the same thing from different companies that are being purchased, there's no way to know what that looks like. So for example, and I love

these companies here, but we have under maintenance supplies that were purchased. We have a purchase from Grainger and a purchase from Home Depot. So separately, those two purchases are under the threshold, but together as one like kind, it comes up to $266,000. Now, I love myself some Home Depot and Grainger, so it's not an issue about what's purchased or whatever, but it's just about being able to look at the like-kind purchases of things. There's a bigger example of this in here, too, about furniture. So there's $1.55 million

in furniture purchases that have happened over the last quarter. And so being able to have furniture and the total amount, and then the vendors that we paid for that would be helpful so we can look and see. And it makes perfect sense that over the summer we would make those kind of purchases. So again, I'm not questioning the purchase itself. It's just more of a way of reporting and having some clarity. So I think you're hitting on some of the challenges that we were working on in pulling this together, which was also

defining purchase versus payment. And I think, because we went around and around, or I went around and around in working with the team, of trying to clearly delineate when we mean purchase, that means purchase order versus a payment, which is like cash went out the door. And those are two very different things, because a purchase order doesn't mean cash has went out. Purchase order could mean zero cash has went out the door.

Right. It's just a commitment, and at the end of the day, it could be substantially less cash out the door related to what was listed on here on that first report. So we could have a PO for something for 600,000, and by the end of the fourth quarter, the actual payment, maybe it shows up on the other report, may only be 200,000. And so I'm wondering too, as we work through this policy of

trying to clearly identify exactly what we are all meaning, so that we're talking the same language and that way we can provide the specific information. I did want to add too, just a couple of things. Number one, I believe earlier you had said something about competition. All the procurement methods except sole source have competition. Right. So I did want to clarify that. The next thing is on furniture.

Although furniture sounds similar, it's not. There's student furniture, there's admin furniture, there's music furniture. Those are different types of vendors. And furniture, in those cases, we use cooperatives for furniture. We have found that cooperatives definitely give us the best pricing because we can reap the benefits of a cooperative that serves the entire country. And also that when you say similar or like,

that's a matter of because, like I said, a director's stand is different than a student desk. And that is how granular, if we have the NIGP code working correctly in Oracle, that is how granular this gets. And that is how the procurement methods work as well. Therefore, that is why I grouped them at the higher level. Mm-hmm. And there may be multiple vendors under furniture, but they

provide very different types of furniture. Yeah. I think for right now, since we're not in the new system, that's perfectly fine, and if it becomes easier to delineate once we get into the new system, then we can break the system down further. And I appreciate the clarification on that. So there's things like musical instruments too, and I'm sure some of these are actual purchasing instruments versus repair of them too. I know there's pieces of that too, right? So- Those are two different LCPS contracts. Yes. Yeah, absolutely. So I get that there are subsets.

The descriptions are very big picture, and I'm okay with that for now. Once we get into a system where it's easier to report the subcategories, I think that would be helpful. But for now, just to get this as a first step in the process in our current system, because when are we going to get into Oracle, and when do we think we'd be able to even... I'm not holding you, by the way, to a deadline. I'm just curious. So our phase one, which is our financials, goes live July 1, 2027. But then there's a subcomponent

related to procurement, and I'll let Ms. Viglia give you the specific dates. We have the financials going live July 1, 2027, and then in October, November, we begin working on the sourcing component of Oracle Fusion, which is the potential to do our solicitations through Oracle Fusion as well, which will bring us more detail directly into the Oracle system. In addition, the purchase card

does not use commodity codes. So that adds a whole other element- Yeah ... to some of the manual work that we need to do to get things mirrored up. Because you would need to do that anyway, though, for your own internal- We do that internally- Yeah ... by various means. One of the things I wanted to share is, for example, when it uses a purchase order, we see every requisition. I approve and review every

requisition. So before it even becomes a purchase order, I review the request for the purchase to make sure it is in compliance with all of our requirements. Monthly, we run a vendor spend based on spend across those three groups. We look at the spend to ensure that we have a procurement method identified for that vendor that is one of our procurement methods in policy 4320. We also make sure that annually, my team reviews

every single P-card transaction for a department at least once, if not more than once. So we do have mechanisms in place that we use to track and monitor this. Okay. So you're saying October 27 is when... 27? That's when it starts. I think it's not live. I think it's like March of 2028 or something. Yeah. There's overlap

there. So that'll be interesting because we'll be bringing that one up while we're getting used to the new system, and so yes. Totally get it. Yep, absolutely. Okay. So if I was to kind of move forward a little bit, so in looking at spending with one company and then the sole source piece of this, right? So the policy also asks staff to tell us when the spending with any one company passes 150 a year, and in many cases, that may be the case. We've got a bunch of them in here right now. So

being able to see it, I think, really matters because there's a couple of organizations on here, and if we take one example, like Touch Math, for example, LCPS posts every sole source award on the website, which we mentioned earlier. Right now, that list shows four separate Touch Math awards between July 10th and August 4th. Two were on the same day on July 10th, for about 104,000 each. So together, those four come to

just under $270,000. But none of them was large enough to appear on the large list of purchases. So being able to have that kind of insight, I think, would be really helpful. Again, I don't have any issues with the purchases because they're done however they need to be done, but I think that's the kind of stuff that helps us be able to say, "Okay, we've got a pretty large purchase," and raise whatever questions we may want to in that process. And there's a couple other ones in here too, but I think that's

the kind of stuff that would be really helpful to be able to see. The reason you're seeing them separated on the sole source, just so you know, is we list those by purchase order on sole source. That means a different department ordered. We had two departments that ordered Touch Math, so that was two separate purchase orders. That's an example of what Ms. Willoughby shared as well, where it may not show up on the purchase order list, but once it's paid, it would show up there. The other thing is, when we do these requisitions and so on, we

ensure that the budget is set aside for these purchases, and these were approved purchases through the budget process. Touch Math was done through a grant. We got a grant for some funding for some special programs, and that was how we purchased the Touch Math. Okay. That would be really helpful then probably to see on there too, is not just the procurement, but if it's grant money, it's a separate kind of thing. But I don't want to get things too jumbled, but

that tells me something very different than as part of our regular budget versus it being grant money that it's going to come and go and has a set window of usage. But again, I don't want to go down too many rabbit holes on this so we'll keep that. And like I said, I'm going to send you guys an email just to make sure we got some of this squared away. So the other one about the sole sources across

the report. So our policies allow for sole source purchasing when staff document in writing that there's only one company that can practically provide that resource. Is that correct? What we do on sole sources is we get a letter from the company that says they are the only vendor. You can only buy it directly from them. They do not have resellers. And then we also have the budget holder do a sole source justification. Why is it sole source? Why does it best meet your needs?

How does it compare to other items that may be out on the market that are somewhat comparable, but not exactly this? We have an entire process we go through. In addition, on sole sources cooperative, we also have an LCPS contract we create that we sign, the vendor signs with all our terms and conditions in it. So we do have a rigorous process in place before we determine something is sole source. The first thing staff will do because of timing is if we don't have an

LCPS solicitation, they'll look for a cooperative, because the cooperatives have been competitively bid. I actually was fortunate to serve on one of these one time for a national contract. It's a very detailed process. It's very similar to what we do today with our own LCPS RFPs and IFBs as well. Mm-hmm. So I've noticed just in the sole source process and of the list, for example, College Board, which obviously does our testing, and we've been doing a lot of it here early on.

So we've got 184 sole source awards in the first quarter. It's about $15.8 million that's been awarded, and I get it. A lot of it is College Board stuff. We've got staff training. We've got athletic officials. It's just really, I think, for me, from a board perspective, really interesting to see all the things and the timeline of when we make these purchases. We do have the ability though to go back and look at what we did in the first

quarter of last year. So it would be really great to be able to pull some of that data and be able to look at the historical aspects of it now, not having to wait into next year before we have two years of this data under this policy. We've got data that we can go back and pull, I would hope. I would just like to remind the committee that the team is juggling multiple tasks right now with their normal workload, in addition to implementing the project that you just heard has multiple phases.

And so I'm very protective of trying to prioritize staff's time, knowing that right now there is a lot happening within business and financial services. And so that is why we have approached this with the mindset of this point going forward. Again, just in terms of workload management, the team is truly beyond capacity, managing their daily duties, closing year-end,

starting up the new fiscal year, and implementing the Fusion project. And I will add, when you're looking at the sole source list and timing, actually the fact that we have those numbers of purchase orders and sole source is a good thing because we always ask them, encumber the funds so they're available when the invoice comes in. So staff is doing a very good job of the things that are outlined in their budget of getting those encumbered. Your officials, for example.

We know we're going to need wrestling officials, basketball officials. So they're all doing a very good job of exactly what we've asked them to do, is to set aside the funds, which is a policy requirement, for the purchases for when the invoicing comes in. So that's why you're seeing that as well. Yeah, and I can appreciate. Again, I don't have any issues about the purchases that are being made. This isn't about that. It's about us fulfilling our responsibility for financial management of the budget And having some transparency and insight into

the expenses and how they're being managed, or how they're being spent, and what we're spending the money on. And it's becoming more important, I think, for us to be really crystal clear about that, because we are getting into a tighter financial situation with our budget, and we've got to understand where the money is being spent so that we can figure out do we want to continue with those expenses and those procurements and whatnot, or do we need to start looking at places where we can cut back a little

bit or cut out completely if that is the will of the board? So again, this isn't about being critical of how we've been spending the money. It's about having some more clarity about the depth of that so that we can figure out, as we're looking at the budget long term, how we're going to wind up either going breakeven or whatever the situation's going to wind up being this coming year and in the years out from this. And I get the staffing concerns, too.

I will tell you, if you have the raw data, I can pull it together. I think that there are tools that we have available to us that we can do to help craft this with the spirit of the policy in mind and be able to look at the historical data. If I made a request, and we had board members that asked for it, we could get the raw data and do the analysis. But I would really like this to come from the finance team, because you all have the context of it.

And I get that you're busy, and we've got a lot of projects going. But at the same time, we also have some requirements on our end of fulfilling our financial duties, and I want to make sure that we have time to do that as well. So- I would just like to, if I may add, that similar to other financial reporting that has been asked of my department, raw data, I love how you describe that, because I think it's a

perfect example of what we're talking about and the work that it takes to take that raw data to then make it be consumable and understandable by the committee and public. The example I would like to give is that our team is a team of experts in their fields and using the systems that we have. They are well-versed in speaking what I would call the finance language, the procurement language,

meaning the reports and data that they are using, that raw data, is very much numeric. We could spit out reports. I could give you a report that's going to have 13 segments and have, I can't remember how many numbers is in our account string, and it will be gobbledygook to the public. It takes time to translate those segments into what the department is, what the fund is, what a vendor name is, even

perhaps the procurement method. It could be all coding in the system. Not all this data is necessarily in a format where it's easily produced. And so that's where when we talk about the time and when this policy was first revised, adding these reporting requirements was really about that piece. And so I wouldn't want to oversimplify the process that it takes to take the raw data and the volume of the raw data,

and to make it in a consumable format for the committee. Sure. I understand that. But I'm going to also just tell you really simply, having just the data that we've got here in the last couple of hours, or actually this morning, and really diving into this, I'm able to even create simple tables that tell me of all of the data that you've got for sole sourcing, that we've got 13 awards on testing and assessment at $5 million. This is the kind of stuff, big picture, that helps me make a decision about

what's going on. Or just to simply ask questions. We had 27 awards for staff training and consultation at $1.3 million. Okay. It's the beginning of the school year, and I get that there's a lot of professional development. This is the kind of stuff that helps us do our job better, and I don't know. I would like to see that kind of reporting coming out of the finance team so that we can make decisions. If it's going to be a thing where we've got to get the data

from you and do our own analysis, we can do that. But I would hope that we could look at this policy and understand it from the lens of the school board that we're needing to start taking a look at some of these things from a big picture perspective, and relatively quickly now because we're in the budget season, start understanding a bit more about what we're actually spending our money on. And again, it's not a value judgment of is it a good or a bad spend, but at

some point in time, again, we're going to have to get really serious about the finances that we're looking at, and we've got to have some deeper window into what's actually being spent so that we can figure out where we're going to start cutting back or start adjusting for budget purposes. We've got to find a middle ground here where we're able to get the data that we need in order to make good decisions from a board perspective and not overburdening you all with a whole bunch of

additional data requests. Which was one of the purposes of this policy, is to be able to get the data that we need in order to help make those decisions. Noted. And I'll just end by saying that we are reporting and meeting the requirements that's outlined in the policy. Okay. And I would just say that I don't agree. I think there's some pieces of it that are missing. But I think what I'm going to do, instead of taking more time on this, is I'll send an email with all of these and see if we

can find a middle ground on this, and I would like to see, hopefully, a revised report at the next F&O so we can make sure that we're on the same page moving forward. Thank you I would just, in response to that, again, we have provided the report in response to the policy, and we have provided our quarterly notification to the F&O Committee.

Thank you, everyone. Thank you, Ms. Ricardi, for all these details that you pulled from these reports. I really appreciate it. I do agree that with budget constraints coming up, it's going to happen. We are going to scrutinize the budget, and it's just how it's going to go, unfortunately.

And with that, I'd like to ask what my colleagues think should be the next step for this policy. Oh, Mr. Pepe. Go ahead. Thank you, Madam Chair.
